title: Shantala Devi Keeps Her Faith
subtitle: A Jain Queen in a Changing Hoysala World
region: Belur, Halebidu, Balligavi, Shivagange and Shravanabelagola
moral: Integrity can shine even inside a changing court.

sources.note: Primary record of Shantala Devi's sallekhana, family, guru and grants.

sources.citation: Belur and Shravanabelagola inscriptions in Epigraphia Carnatica
sources.note: Primary evidence for royal women and Jain patronage.
Modern documentation of Shantala Devi and Hoysala patronage.

panels.shot: epic wide of Shantala Devi standing between Belur temple towers and Chandragiri hill, dusk light dividing the frame

dialogue.text: In an age when Hoysalas turned to new gods and new wars, Queen Shantala Devi walked a different path—writing her Jain faith into stone, and choosing her own final fast.

panels.shot: slow aerial drift over Malnad hills and river valleys at sunrise

dialogue.text: The Hoysala realm wakes in the early 1100s—hill forts in the Malnad, temple towns in the plains, Jain basadis and Shaiva and Vaishnava shrines sharing the same red earth.

panels.shot: wide shot of Hoysala court at Dvarasamudra, king on throne, courtiers arrayed

dialogue.text: Vishnuvardhana, Hoysala king, pushes his frontier against the Cholas and celebrates with stone—commissioning temples at Belur and Dvarasamudra, filling their walls with stories in soapstone.

panels.shot: medium shot of Shantala Devi in the royal hall, slightly apart from the court

dialogue.text: Beside him sits his mahadevi, Shantala Devi. Inscriptions name her not as shadow, but with lineage, grants, devotion, and a voice of her own.

panels.shot: close-up on Shantala Devi’s hands and veena, soft light from a lattice window

dialogue.text: One record calls her a master of music and dance. It is praise, not gossip. We do not see her perform, but we hear echoes of skill that impressed her age.

panels.shot: wide shot of Belur temple courtyard bustling with artisans, Shantala Devi arriving in palanquin

dialogue.text: At Belur, the great Vaishnava temple grows. Yet nearby a more modest shrine, Kappe Chennigaraya, carries her name—one of several works linked to her patronage.

panels.shot: low-angle view of Shantala Devi examining stone panels, sculptors nearby

dialogue.text: She moves among sculptors, not as mere observer, but as donor. Inscriptions show royal women choosing sites, endowments, and the very gods their gifts would serve.

panels.shot: medium shot inside a Jain basadi, Shantala Devi before a Jina image

dialogue.text: Yet inside her, another thread runs clear. In Shravanabelagola and other records she appears as a Jain donor, placing gifts before Jinas, guided by a Jain acharya.

panels.shot: close-up on Shantala Devi listening to Jain guru Prabhachandra (shown only as robed figure)

dialogue.text: Her inscription names Prabhachandra Siddhanta Deva as guru. Under his guidance she supports Jain establishments, while her husband’s court leans strongly toward Vaishnava temples.

panels.shot: wide shot of Halebidu twin temple complex, one side subtly associated with Shantala

dialogue.text: At Dvarasamudra, the Shantalesvara shrine bears her name. Again, stone remembers a queen whose agency was strong enough to be shared in the main temple form.

panels.shot: medium shot of Shantala Devi at a court grant ceremony, scribes writing on palm-leaf

dialogue.text: Record my gift, so that even after me, the lamps will not go dark.

panels.shot: close-up on palm-leaf manuscript being inscribed, Shantala Devi faintly reflected in a metal vessel

dialogue.text: We know her from such words. Epigraphia Carnatica preserves these grants, where her name stands beside villages, tanks, and income set aside for Jain worship and service.

panels.shot: low-angle interior of Belur temple, Shantala Devi walking past Vaishnava icons

dialogue.text: Shantala Devi lives in a plural house. She does not renounce her Jain faith to match her husband; instead she inhabits a court where multiple religious currents run side by side.

panels.shot: medium shot of aging Shantala Devi on Chandragiri hill, gazing at Gommateshwara in distance

dialogue.text: By 1131, her path nears its end. On Chandragiri hill at Shravanabelagola, she prepares for sallekhana—the Jain fast unto death, undertaken as a final act of discipline and detachment.

panels.shot: close-up on Shantala Devi’s calm face as she begins the fast, sky behind her

dialogue.text: May this body fade softly, and may my vows remain steady.

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder shot of stone inscription being carved on Chandragiri, Shantala seated in background

dialogue.text: As she fasts, her life is carved into stone—the Chandragiri inscription noting her family, her guru, her gifts, and this chosen manner of passing from the world.

panels.shot: wide shot of Chandragiri hill at dusk, Shantala small against sweeping landscape

dialogue.text: Her death, like her life, is recorded plainly. No later legend of conversion or conflict replaces the simple fact: a Jain queen remained Jain to the end.

panels.shot: slow push-in on weathered Chandragiri inscription, letters worn but legible

dialogue.text: Centuries later, scholars like S. Settar read those lines again, seeing there one of medieval Karnataka’s clearest records of a queen’s agency and spiritual choice.

panels.shot: final wide shot blending Belur temple and Chandragiri hill in one composition, Shantala as faint overlay

dialogue.text: Shantala Devi’s story reminds us that even inside powerful courts, integrity can persist—quiet, inscribed in grants and stone, holding its faith while kingdoms shift around it.
